summary: International education this week has four main threads. First, China–UK education cooperation has restarted: after nine years, a China–UK education ministers' consultation and education summit were held in Beijing on 24–25 November. The two sides signed an Agreement on Strengthening Cooperation in Education, covering nine areas including higher education, cross-border education, and digital and artificial intelligence, and established three working groups on digital education, STEM basic education and vocational education. The University of Liverpool in the same period announced four new transnational-education partnerships with Hebei University of Technology, Ocean University of China, Southern Medical University and Tianjin University. Second, AI is reshaping university teaching and resource allocation: EPFL is advancing the s’ÉPanouir-FLourish curriculum reform and has been selected as XPRIZE's first innovation hub on the European continent (7.5 million Swiss francs over five years); the Lilly Endowment in the United States approved a total of $291.71 million in "AI in Higher Education" implementation grants for 35 institutions in Indiana. Third, study-abroad policy is tightening and loosening at once: US courts have successively vacated or frozen new rules limiting international students' duration of stay and CPT internships, but an OPT-fee rule is still under review; Canada is keeping a target of 150,000 new international students a year; South Korea plans to tie work and post-graduation residence rights to Korean-language proficiency. Fourth, talent training in quantum and frontier technology is moving into national and international programmes: India's first "quantum–AI university" transitional campus has opened in Guntur, with classes starting on 1 December; NYU Abu Dhabi, with US State Department funding, has launched a lunar-exploration instrument training programme for 30 Emirati and American graduate students.
trends: China–UK and China–Europe education cooperation has seen an institutional restart: an intergovernmental agreement lists "digital and artificial intelligence" as a field of cooperation, and UK universities are accelerating joint colleges and transnational education in China, with medicine, life sciences and AI as priorities.

AI is pushing universities from "using tools" toward "reshaping curricula and institutions": EPFL is redesigning programmes and teaching incentives, and a US private foundation is driving AI transformation across a state's universities with staged, large-scale funding.

Study-abroad policy is tightening and loosening at once: US courts have temporarily stabilised study and internship pathways, but OPT remains uncertain; Canada is keeping a low quota; South Korea is turning toward management centred on language ability and educational quality.

Quantum and AI talent training is moving into specialised national institutions (India's NIELIT quantum–AI campus), with degree education and large-scale skills certification in parallel, and tied to an industrial park (Quantum Valley).

Internationally mixed, mission-driven, open-source graduate programmes (NYUAD lunar exploration) and international-challenge hubs (XPRIZE in Switzerland) are becoming a new form connecting education, research and social impact.
footer: All facts and figures in this brief come from the public sources listed (publication dates are given in each item). Compiled by QCF's chief development officer (008 QCF COO) for internal decision-making reference; this does not constitute investment or legal advice.

items.title: A China–UK education summit restarts in Beijing after nine years: a cooperation agreement covering nine fields is signed and three working groups are set up; the University of Liverpool announces four new China–UK joint programmes
items.what: According to China's Ministry of Education on 25 November, a China–UK education ministers' consultation restarted in Beijing on 24 November after nine years, with Minister of Education Huai Jinpeng meeting UK Secretary of State for Education Lucy Powell. The two sides agreed to hold regular ministerial dialogues, established under that framework three working groups on digital education, STEM basic education and vocational education, and signed an Agreement on Strengthening Cooperation in Education, setting out cooperation in nine fields: preschool, basic, vocational, higher, cross-border and lifelong education, special education, language education, and digital and artificial intelligence. A UK government notice on 23 November said about 150,000 Chinese students are studying at UK universities and contributed £7 billion to the UK economy last year; the UK delegation had 49 people, including 18 university leaders; the UK side also said it would discuss academic freedom and national-security concerns frankly. The University of Liverpool announced on 24 November four transnational-education partnerships approved by China's Ministry of Education: Liverpool College of Hebei University of Technology (six undergraduate majors, four master's majors admitting from 2027); an undergraduate law programme between Ocean University of China and the University of Liverpool (first cohort of 120); an undergraduate stomatology partnership with Southern Medical University (admitting from July 2027); and Liverpool Fuzhou Joint College of Tianjin University (including an undergraduate programme in intelligent medical engineering).
items.why: This is the most important institutional restart of China–UK education relations in nearly a decade, and "digital and artificial intelligence" has been formally written into the fields of cooperation. UK universities are shifting China cooperation from recruitment toward transnational education and joint colleges in China, with life sciences, medicine and AI as priorities.
items.src: Ministry of Education of the People's Republic of China; GOV.UK (UK Department for Education); University of Liverpool News

items.tag: Curriculum reform in the AI era / innovation hubs
items.title: EPFL advances a curriculum reshaping for the AI era; XPRIZE selects EPFL for its first innovation hub on the European continent (7.5 million Swiss francs over five years)
items.what: On 24 November EPFL described its s’ÉPanouir-FLourish curriculum reform: the plan was launched a year ago by the Vice Presidency for Education and is advanced through five working groups with faculty and student participation. Each school will redesign its programmes, with a focus on first-year foundations in mathematics, physics and computational thinking, methods of learning and assessment, project-based learning, and the creation of a teaching-development fund. Vice President for Education Nicolas Grandjean said AI is prompting the school to rethink programmes and to address academic workload; a survey of 229 faculty members found that teachers do not believe teaching quality is sufficiently recognised in career promotion. The next event is set for 9 December. According to an EPFL release on 25 November, XPRIZE has selected EPFL as its Swiss hub and first hub on the European continent (the second international hub after Canada in 2025). The five-year programme has 7.5 million Swiss francs behind it, connecting researchers, students, start-ups and the public sector, and focusing on global challenges in energy and climate, health, deep tech, learning and society; the hub will formally start next year.
items.why: A leading Swiss technical university, under the impact of AI, is shifting its emphasis from transmitting knowledge toward foundational skills, project practice and teaching incentives, and is using an international competition platform to turn research into social impact.

items.title: The Lilly Endowment approves $291.71 million in "AI in Higher Education" grants for 35 institutions in Indiana, toward a $500 million programme
items.what: Lilly Endowment announced on 23 November that it had approved 35 implementation grants through its Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education (AIHE) programme, of $2.5 million to $25 million each (set by enrolment size), totalling $291,710,000. The grants will support faculty AI-capability development, technical infrastructure, AI policy and governance, ethical frameworks, research on the social and economic impact of AI, and adjustments to curricula and career development. Institutions already received planning grants in December 2025; the foundation expects to approve in December further grants supporting large-scale collaboration among two or more institutions, taking total AIHE appropriations to $500 million. Foundation vice president Ted Maple said the rapid spread of AI may be one of the most significant challenges universities face, and may also bring unprecedented opportunities for teaching, student services and research.
items.why: This is one of the largest private-foundation programmes to date aimed at AI transformation across a state's universities, using a staged design of planning grants, implementation grants and cross-institution collaboration grants — a sign that philanthropic capital is shifting from named buildings toward institutional capacity-building.

items.title: US courts vacate a fixed duration-of-stay rule for international students and freeze tightening of CPT, while an OPT fee remains pending; Canada keeps a target of 150,000 new international students a year
items.what: Inside Higher Ed surveyed the situation on 24 November: a DHS rule that would have replaced "duration of status" (D/S) with a fixed term (generally four years, with an extension application required) was vacated in full by a court last week (NAFSA gives the judgment date as 16 November), and the government is appealing; guidance restricting curricular practical training (CPT) has been temporarily frozen by a judge, and many universities have resumed processing CPT, though some still follow the August memoranda; a proposed rule that would require universities to pay a fee for OPT applications (reports say as much as more than $70,000 per student) has not been finalised, and the public-comment period ended on 9 November. According to Reuters (reprinted by BNN Bloomberg on 25 November), Canada's latest immigration plan sets 150,000 new international students a year for the next three years, well below 292,830 in 2024; new international students in January–July 2026 were down 80% from the same period in 2024. Joseph Wong, vice-president international at the University of Toronto, said the study-permit cap had "damaged Canada's brand"; international enrolment at Humber Polytechnic has fallen to about one-third of 2023/24, with a C$40 million revenue gap.
items.why: Policy uncertainty remains high in North America's two main study-abroad destinations: US courts have temporarily stabilised study and internship pathways, but the post-graduation work pathway (OPT) is still in flux; Canada, while limiting undergraduate and college enrolment, is trying to attract high-end talent with research funding.
items.src: Inside Higher Ed; NAFSA; Reuters / BNN Bloomberg

items.title: International students in South Korea already exceed 307,000, ahead of target; the government plans to tie work and post-graduation residence rights to Korean-language proficiency
items.what: According to The Korea Times on 26 November, there were 307,464 international students in South Korea as of April this year, already ahead of the government's 2027 target of 300,000. A draft under study at the Ministry of Justice proposes that international students who do not meet Korean-language requirements would lose the current permission to work 10 hours a week, and that English proficiency would no longer serve as a basis for work rights; Korean-language level may also determine the length of stay on a D-10 job-seeking visa (currently up to three years). The scheme has not been finalised, and a 2–3 year transition is proposed. The Ministry of Education plans to publish a reform of the "international education quality certification system" between December and January, to take effect in 2029, giving priority to academic standards, language ability and educational outcomes rather than enrolment numbers, and considering linking it to institutional accreditation and tightening visa review for financially strained institutions.
items.why: An emerging Asian study-abroad destination, after rapid growth in scale, is turning toward quality and integration. Language ability and educational quality are becoming core indicators for visas and accreditation.

items.title: India's first "quantum–AI university" campus opens in Guntur: classes start on 1 December, with a five-year plan to train about 8,250 people
items.what: According to India Today on 23 November (and The Hindu on 21 November), the National Institute of Electronics and Information Technology (NIELIT), under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), opened a transitional campus on Saturday 21 November at Acharya Nagarjuna University in Guntur, Andhra Pradesh, described as India's first university campus focused on quantum computing and artificial intelligence. Training courses are set to start on 1 December, covering quantum computing, quantum communications, scientific and engineering AI, chip design/VLSI, embedded systems and the Internet of Things. NIELIT will invest 47 crore rupees in four advanced laboratories; the permanent campus is in Amaravati, on 8.5 acres, with approved investment of 730.70 crore rupees. The campus plans to train about 8,250 people over five years, 1,650 in degree programmes and 6,600 in skills and certification courses, and will offer undergraduate, master's, doctoral and diploma programmes. Students are expected to have access to an IBM quantum computer deployed under the Amaravati Quantum Valley programme.
items.why: State-led universities that fuse quantum, AI and semiconductors are beginning to appear, with degree education and large-scale skills certification in parallel. Quantum talent training is moving from research universities toward specialised national institutions.

items.title: NYU Abu Dhabi launches a "Lunar Exploration Pioneers" programme: 30 mixed Emirati and American graduate students design science payloads for a lunar rover
items.what: According to Gulf News on 25 November, New York University Abu Dhabi (NYUAD), with funding from the US Department of State, has launched an 18-month Lunar Exploration Pioneers programme (starting this month) to train 30 graduate students, half from UAE and half from US universities, mixed into six teams, each designing and building a science payload for a lunar rover developed by NYUAD, from early design through to a calibrated prototype. The teams will test for two weeks in NYUAD's Saadiyat lunar laboratory using an "Emirati lunar-regolith simulant" made from UAE rocks, and carry out further resource characterisation at the Colorado School of Mines in the United States; the best team will visit a NASA centre and a commercial lunar-exploration company. The programme aims to produce six tested instruments, of which up to three will enter a preliminary design phase, and to create an open-source technical-challenge pack. The programme lead is Dr Dimitra Atri of NYUAD's Center for Astrophysics and Space Science.
items.why: Middle Eastern universities are training graduate students in frontier science and technology through internationally mixed teams, real missions and open-source outputs, with intergovernmental funding and a transnational campus network as key supports.
